subtype: Approach: asking why it hurts so much [Thinking]
passage: The pressure cooker was whistling and Mahima's mother had ten minutes before leaving for work, but she stopped stirring when Mahima muttered, "Akash says I'm stupid." "Which word hurts most?" her mother asked, turning down the flame. Mahima thought. Not "stupid". It was the way people laughed. "Why does the laughing hurt?" "Because maybe he's right." Then she frowned. "But I got full marks in spelling on Monday. So what Akash thinks isn't the truth about me. It's only his opinion." Her mother nodded and said she would phone the class teacher that evening, since grown-ups would deal with what Akash did. Mahima's chest felt lighter as the cooker whistled again.

qa.q: What was whistling in the kitchen while Mahima spoke to her mother?
qa.a: The pressure cooker was whistling.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she said the laughing hurt, and what lay underneath?
qa.a: She felt hurt and a little afraid, because underneath she worried that Akash might be right about her.

qa.q: What other approach could help Mahima alongside thinking it over, and why?
qa.a: She could stay near friends and tell the teacher each time it happens, because thinking eases the hurt but adults are the ones who can stop the behaviour.

qa.q: How might Mahima's mother feel about stopping to listen with only ten minutes left?
qa.a: Probably worried and caring, since she turned down the flame, asked a question and promised to phone the class teacher.

grounding: A girl works out which words hurt and why, decides the bully's opinion does not define her, and adults deal with the behaviour.

subtype: Approach: choosing the right moment and mood [Thinking]
passage: Emeka had the question ready at four o'clock: could he sleep over at Tobi's on Saturday? But Dad had just walked in with his shoulders low, phone pressed to his ear, talking about invoices. Not now, Emeka thought. Dad says yes when he is easy, not when he is tired. So Emeka did his reading, set the table and dried the plates. After dinner Dad leaned back with his tea and started the crossword. That was the moment. "Dad, have you got time for a small question?" Emeka asked. Dad looked up, smiling. "Go on." It was not yes yet, but it was "Tell me about it", and that was a start.

qa.q: What was Dad doing when Emeka asked his question?
qa.a: Dad was leaning back with his tea, starting the crossword.

qa.q: What was Emeka thinking about Dad's mood at four o'clock?
qa.a: He thought Dad was too tired and busy to say yes, because Dad says yes when he is easy and not when he is tired, so Emeka decided to wait.

qa.q: What else could Emeka prepare so the request goes well?
qa.a: He could have the details ready, such as where Tobi lives and when he will be home, since Dad is likely to ask about them.

qa.q: How might Dad have felt if Emeka had asked during the phone call?
qa.a: Probably irritated and distracted, since Dad was tired and busy, and he might have said no just to end the interruption.

grounding: A boy waits until his father is relaxed after dinner before asking about a sleepover.

subtype: Approach: preparing reasons and answers to objections [Action]
passage: I live next door to Leela, and on Saturday I watched her at the balcony table with a pencil, writing a list. She let me read it. Why I need a bicycle: school is twenty minutes on foot and the library is farther. How I will stay safe: helmet, only the lane behind our building, home before dusk. What I will do: keep my birthday money and wash Papa's car for a month toward the cost. Then she practised aloud, "But what if you fall?", and answered herself. At dinner time she went in with the paper folded small. Her fingers looked tight around it. I don't know what her parents said, but she walked in ready. Sarika

qa.q: What three things did Leela put on her list of ways to stay safe?
qa.a: A helmet, riding only in the lane behind the building, and being home before dusk.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt as she went in with the paper, according to Sarika?
qa.a: Nervous but prepared, since her fingers looked tight around the paper, though Sarika cannot be sure what Leela felt. 🙂

qa.q: What could Leela try if her parents still say no?
qa.a: She could ask what would change their answer or suggest a trial period, because it shows she is willing to work toward what they need.

qa.q: How might Leela's parents see a written list compared with a plain request?
qa.a: They might see it as a sign that she has thought about safety and cost, so they have real points to discuss rather than only a demand.

grounding: A girl lists why she needs a bicycle, how she will be safe and how she will help pay, and rehearses the questions.

subtype: Approach: nagging and repeating the demand [Pitfall]
passage: Every afternoon Mina met her mother, Astrid, at the door with the same words: "Can I have a phone now? Everyone has one." On Monday Astrid said not yet. On Tuesday Mina asked again, louder. On Wednesday she cried on the stairs, and Astrid stayed quiet and firm. On Thursday Mina stamped her foot, and her father said, "Enough. The answer will not change if you ask ten times." By Friday Mina had stopped saying anything at all, and dinner was tense. Astrid's face looked tired more than angry. Mina had never once said why she needed a phone or what she would do to use it carefully.

qa.q: On which day did Mina cry on the stairs?
qa.a: Mina cried on the stairs on Wednesday.

qa.q: What might Mina be feeling as she stamped her foot on Thursday?
qa.a: Frustrated and disappointed, because each refusal made her angrier and asking again was not working.

qa.q: What different approach might have earned Mina a better hearing, and why?
qa.a: She could ask once, calmly at a good moment, with reasons and a plan for using it carefully, because parents can weigh reasons but pressure only makes them firmer.

qa.q: How does Mina's asking look to Astrid by the end of the week?
qa.a: Wearing: Astrid looks tired rather than angry, and every repeat gives her more reason to stay firm.

grounding: A child asks for a phone daily and cries when refused, and the parents grow firmer because pressure gives them no reasons.

passage: Note, Thursday. I look after Rafiq after school, and yesterday I watched him do something new. He asked his parents for ten minutes, sat them down and read from a paper: "If I may have a puppy, I will take it on the morning walk every day before school, and I will keep my marks at least where they were last term." His mother asked who would clean up. Rafiq said, "Me, and I will ask for help at first." His father smiled and called the offer fair, and they said they would think until Sunday. Rafiq nodded quickly, though his knee kept bouncing under the table. I told him waiting is part of the deal. Pooja

qa.q: What two things did Rafiq promise in return for a puppy?
qa.a: He promised to take it on the morning walk every day before school and to keep his marks at least where they were last term.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling while he waited for his parents' answer?
qa.a: Nervous and hopeful, since his knee kept bouncing under the table even though he nodded quickly.

qa.q: What could Rafiq add to his offer if his parents remain unsure?
qa.a: He could suggest a trial period or offer some pocket money for supplies, because it lowers the risk for his parents.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's parents see the proposal compared with a plain "please"?
qa.a: It gives them something concrete to weigh, and his father called it fair, so they seem to see a child ready to take responsibility.

grounding: A boy offers his parents a deal, morning walks and steady marks, in exchange for a pet.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing the request with a sibling [Thinking]
passage: Papa's scooter would be back in twenty minutes, so Iram pulled her older brother Samir into the front room. "You be Papa. I ask for the trip with my friends." Samir folded his arms and dropped his voice. "A day trip? Who is going? Who is driving? Why should I trust this?" "Everyone is going!" Iram said. Samir shook his head. "That is the weakest thing you can say." Iram groaned, then tried again: the names of the friends, two grown-ups coming, the bus timings, her phone in her pocket. Samir gave one stern nod. "Better." The scooter horn sounded early, and Iram wiped her palms on her kurta.

qa.q: Which argument did Samir call the weakest one?
qa.a: He called "Everyone is going!" the weakest thing Iram could say.

qa.q: What was Iram feeling when the scooter horn sounded early?
qa.a: Nervous, since she wiped her palms on her kurta as her practice time ran out. 😅

qa.q: What other way could Iram prepare, and why would it help?
qa.a: She could write down the plan with names, timings and the bus route to hand to her parents, because they can read it slowly and she will not forget details.

qa.q: How might Samir see his part as the strict father?
qa.a: He seems to take it seriously, giving real objections and a nod when the answers improved, so he probably wants Iram to succeed.

grounding: A girl practises a trip request on her older brother, who plays a strict father, and learns which arguments sound weak.

subtype: Approach: accepting a no and asking what would change it [Revision]
passage: Friday. Suraj asked to stay at the fair with his friends until ten. His mother, Reena, said no. Suraj's jaw tightened, but he took a breath. "Okay. What would I have to show you for a late outing to be a yes?" His father looked surprised. "Trust," Reena said. "Start with smaller outings, home on time, and we will see." Sunday. Suraj went to the park with his friends and was home at six, exactly as agreed. Two weeks later, a film with his cousins; he was back when he had said. This time Reena asked, "Would you like to try the fair next month?" Suraj grinned and said he would be home by nine.

qa.q: What did Reena say Suraj would need to show for a late outing?
qa.a: She said Suraj would need to show trust, starting with smaller outings and being home on time.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling right after hearing no, and how did he handle it?
qa.a: Disappointed, as his tightened jaw showed, but he took a breath and asked calmly what would change the answer.

qa.q: What could Suraj do if he came home late once during the trial?
qa.a: Tell his parents honestly why and offer to repeat the smaller outing, because honesty protects the trust he is building.

qa.q: How might Suraj's father have felt when Suraj asked his question?
qa.a: Surprised and probably impressed, since he looked surprised that a calm question followed a no.

grounding: A boy told no to a late outing asks what would change it and follows the small-steps answer his parents give.

subtype: Approach: asking a grandparent to speak first [Action]
passage: Note for Mrs Rao at the art school. Usha came to me on Sunday and whispered that she wants art classes but is afraid to ask her parents, because they listen to me. I said I would mention it first, on Monday, over tea. I did: I said only that Usha has been drawing every day and might enjoy a class. Her mother said, "Let us hear from Usha." At dinner Usha spoke up about the colours she wants to learn with, the timings after school, and how she will keep her homework done. Her father asked about the fees, so we plan to visit your class on Saturday. Nani

qa.q: What did Nani say she would mention on Monday over tea?
qa.a: Nani would mention that Usha has been drawing every day and might enjoy a class.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she whispered to Nani on Sunday?
qa.a: Afraid of asking her parents directly, which is why she whispered and wanted Nani to speak first.

qa.q: What other approach could help Usha if her parents remain unsure?
qa.a: She could offer to try a few sessions or show them her drawings, because it gives them something to see before a bigger decision.

qa.q: How might Usha's mother have felt when Nani mentioned the idea?
qa.a: Open to it but wanting to hear from Usha herself, since she said "Let us hear from Usha", which suggests she cares what Usha wants. 🙂

grounding: A child asks her grandmother to raise the art-class idea first, then adds her own reasons at dinner.

subtype: Approach: hiding the request and doing it anyway [Pitfall]
passage: Note, Monday. I run the cycle repair stall by the main road. Yesterday afternoon I saw Nitin ride past towards the far park, fast, glancing over his shoulder as if he expected someone. He had told nobody, I learned later, because he thought the answer would be no. I phoned his father that evening, since that road has heavy trucks. Nitin's father came for the bicycle, and Nitin stood by the stall very quiet, eyes on his shoes. His father said, "I am not angry about the park. I am sorry I could not trust you to tell me." Today Nitin asked to ride to the near park, and the answer was "Not yet." Zubin

qa.q: Why did Zubin phone Nitin's father?
qa.a: Zubin phoned Nitin's father because the road Nitin rode on has heavy trucks.

qa.q: What did Nitin expect, and how did that show in the way he rode?
qa.a: He expected a no, so he hid the ride, and he glanced over his shoulder as if worried about being seen.

qa.q: What could Nitin have done instead of going without asking, and why?
qa.a: He could have asked his father with a plan for the route and safety, because a no might have become a yes with conditions.

qa.q: How does the episode look to Nitin's father?
qa.a: He seems hurt more by the missing trust than by the ride, since he said he was sorry that he could not trust Nitin to tell him.

grounding: A boy cycles to the far park without asking because he expects a no, and the discovery costs him his father's trust.

subtype: Approach: writing a short letter when speaking feels hard [Action]
passage: Shreya, come and sit. Your mother says you have gone quiet about something. I know that quiet. I am Indu, and when I was a shy girl of eleven I wanted lessons at the town pool, but the words would not come out at the table. So I wrote a note in my best handwriting: "Dear Amma and Appa, I would like to learn swimming. The class is on Tuesday and Friday evenings, there is a lifeguard, and I will finish my homework first. Please think about it." I left it under the salt pot. They read it that night and said nothing, and I lay awake. Next morning Amma only said, "Let us go and see the pool together."

qa.q: Where did Indu leave the note for the parents?
qa.a: Indu left it under the salt pot.

qa.q: How did Indu feel that night after leaving the note?
qa.a: Anxious and hopeful, since Indu lay awake after the parents read it and said nothing.

qa.q: What other approach might work for a shy child, and why?
qa.a: A shy child could ask a relative to mention it first, because it lets a person get started without a face-to-face moment.

qa.q: How might Indu's parents have felt reading the note?
qa.a: Probably touched and thoughtful, since they said nothing that night but next morning suggested visiting the pool together.

grounding: Indu writes a polite note about swimming lessons and leaves it for the parents to think over.
